# Top K Frequent Elements — Explained, One Approach at a Time

     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Arrays & Hashing** · medium · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-elements/)

Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k elements that occur most frequently. Order among the answers does not matter.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
- -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
- 1 <= k <= the number of distinct values in nums
- the answer is unique — no tie spans the k-th place

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [4, 4, 4, 6, 6, 2], k = 2` | `[4, 6]` | — |
| `nums = [9], k = 1` | `[9]` | — |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. Counting is the easy half — a hash map gives you value → count in one pass.
2. Sorting the counts costs O(n log n). Can you avoid comparing counts to each other at all?
3. Counts are bounded by n. Make an array of buckets where bucket[c] holds every value that occurs c times, then read buckets from the top.

</details>

---

## 1. Sort by count

Count, then sort the distinct values by frequency and slice the top k. Simplest to write; the sort is the only thing costing more than linear.

```python
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return sorted(counts, key=counts.get, reverse=True)[:k]
```

**O(n log n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    HashMap<Integer,Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
    for (int num : nums) {
        counts.put(num, counts.getOrDefault(num, 0) + 1);
    }
    List<Integer> keys = new ArrayList<>(counts.keySet());
    Collections.sort(keys, new Comparator<Integer>() {
        public int compare(Integer a, Integer b) {
            return counts.get(b).compareTo(counts.get(a));
        }
    });
    int size = Math.min(k, keys.size());
    int[] result = new int[size];
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        result[i] = keys.get(i);
    }
    return result;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> topKFrequent(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int,int> counts;
    for (int num : nums) {
        counts[num]++;
    }
    vector<int> keys;
    keys.reserve(counts.size());
    for (auto &p : counts) keys.push_back(p.first);
    sort(keys.begin(), keys.end(), [&](int a, int b){return counts[a]>counts[b];});
    int size = min(k, (int)keys.size());
    vector<int> result(size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) result[i] = keys[i];
    return result;
}
```

</details>

## 2. Heap

> **Why now.** Sorting puts every distinct value in order when only k of them are wanted. A heap of size k keeps just the frontrunners, so the cost follows k instead of the whole set of values.

Keep a min-heap of the k most frequent seen while iterating counts. Better than sorting when k ≪ distinct values; stdlib nlargest does exactly this.

```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts, key=counts.get)
```

**O(n log k) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer,Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
    for (int num: nums) counts.put(num, counts.getOrDefault(num,0)+1);
    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Integer,Integer>> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(k, (a,b)->a.getValue()-b.getValue());
    for (Map.Entry<Integer,Integer> e: counts.entrySet()){
        if (pq.size()<k) pq.offer(e);
        else if (e.getValue()>pq.peek().getValue()){ pq.poll(); pq.offer(e);}    }
    int[] res = new int[k];
    int idx=k-1;
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {res[idx--]=pq.poll().getKey();}
    return res;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> topKFrequent(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> counts;
    for (int num : nums) counts[num]++;
    auto cmp = [](const pair<int, int>& a, const pair<int, int>& b) {
        return a.second > b.second;
    };
    priority_queue<pair<int, int>, vector<pair<int, int>>, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);
    for (auto& p : counts) {
        if ((int)pq.size() < k) pq.push(p);
        else if (p.second > pq.top().second) { pq.pop(); pq.push(p); }
    }
    vector<int> res(k);
    int idx = k - 1;
    while (!pq.empty()) { res[idx--] = pq.top().first; pq.pop(); }
    return res;
}
```

</details>

## 3. The one to remember

> **Why now.** The heap still pays a logarithm on every count. Counts are bounded by n, so they can be array indices: bucket the values by count and read the top k off the end, with no comparison sort anywhere.

Count occurrences with a hash map. Then bucket-sort by count: index c of a length n+1 array collects all values appearing exactly c times. Scanning buckets from n down to 1 and collecting values until you have k avoids any comparison sort, because a count can never exceed n.

```python
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = Counter(nums)
    buckets: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
    for value, c in counts.items():
        buckets[c].append(value)
    out: list[int] = []
    for c in range(len(nums), 0, -1):
        for value in buckets[c]:
            out.append(value)
            if len(out) == k:
                return out
    return out
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer,Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
    for (int num : nums) {
        counts.put(num, counts.getOrDefault(num, 0)+1);
    }
    List<List<Integer>> buckets = new ArrayList<>(nums.length+1);
    for (int i=0;i<=nums.length;i++) buckets.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (Map.Entry<Integer,Integer> e : counts.entrySet()) {
        int value=e.getKey(), c=e.getValue();
        buckets.get(c).add(value);
    }
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int c=nums.length;c>=1;c--) {
        for (int val : buckets.get(c)) {
            out.add(val);
            if (out.size()==k) break;
        }
        if (out.size()==k) break;
    }
    int[] res = new int[out.size()];
    for (int i=0;i<out.size();i++) res[i]=out.get(i);
    return res;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> topKFrequent(const vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    unordered_map<int,int> counts;
    for (int num : nums) counts[num]++;
    vector<vector<int>> buckets(nums.size()+1);
    for (auto &p: counts) {
        int value=p.first, c=p.second;
        buckets[c].push_back(value);
    }
    vector<int> out;
    for (int c=nums.size();c>=1;c--) {
        for (int val : buckets[c]) {
            out.push_back(val);
            if ((int)out.size()==k) break;
        }
        if ((int)out.size()==k) break;
    }
    return out;
}
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sort by count | O(n log n) time · O(n) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Heap | O(n log k) time · O(n) space | Sorting puts every distinct value in order when only k of them are wanted. A heap of size k keeps just the frontrunners, so the cost follows k instead of the whole set of values. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(n) space | The heap still pays a logarithm on every count. Counts are bounded by n, so they can be array indices: bucket the values by count and read the top k off the end, with no comparison sort anywhere. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

Order is not part of this answer, so two rungs printing it differently are
both right — compare the contents, not the line.

```python
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent_sort_by_count(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return sorted(counts, key=counts.get, reverse=True)[:k]


import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent_heap(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts, key=counts.get)


from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = Counter(nums)
    buckets: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
    for value, c in counts.items():
        buckets[c].append(value)
    out: list[int] = []
    for c in range(len(nums), 0, -1):
        for value in buckets[c]:
            out.append(value)
            if len(out) == k:
                return out
    return out

APPROACHES = [
    top_k_frequent_sort_by_count,
    top_k_frequent_heap,
    top_k_frequent_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# a tie in frequency and a k that excludes something — [4,4,4,5,5,6,6,6,6] with k=2
CASES = [
    lambda: ([1,1,1,2,2,3], 2),
    lambda: ([1], 1),
    lambda: ([4,4,4,5,5,6,6,6,6], 2),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<36} -> {answers}")
```
